title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate–Verify‑Repair for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks: a Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM generates device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair reused by baseline and guarded), N = 200 paired intents were executed across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns. Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference = 0.02; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (predeclared primary test). An archived paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04] (reported as exploratory distinct from the preregistered confirmatory test). Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, verifier traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived evidence bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation using large language models (LLMs) promises to reduce routine operator effort in network operations (NetOps). However, LLM outputs can include mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, reachability/topology violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that have direct operational consequences (outages, access regressions, security misconfigurations) [1]–[3]. A common mitigation pattern in recent work is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop: produce a draft configuration, run a deterministic verifier that checks mechanically expressible constraints, and optionally request a repair from the LLM guided by localized verifier feedback [2], [4]. Prior demonstrations show that verifier‑grounded repair reduces mechanically checkable errors in constrained prototypes, but open questions remain about scaling GVR across heterogeneous vendor template families, the operational cost (additional model calls) per avoided violation, and the interpretation of paired comparisons when the same initial draft is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate). Motivated by these gaps and by calls for provenance‑traced, emulator‑based evaluations [5], [6], we preregistered and executed a paired, provenance‑traced Mininet emulation study to estimate whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces the per‑intent incidence of operationally detectable policy violations.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps and AIOps research while highlighting evaluation gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype NetOps and adjacent domain studies show LLMs can draft device configurations but commonly introduce syntax/topology or policy errors; verifier‑grounded closed loops recur as mitigation patterns with empirical demonstrations in code and configuration‑like domains [2], [3]. These prior works motivate an evidence‑grounded, paired design that (a) exercises heterogeneous vendor template families and topology patterns, (b) embeds a deterministic validator able to report mechanically checkable violations, and (c) records provider and verifier accounting for cost analysis. We position our contribution as a provenance‑traced, confirmatory paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics that quantifies the verifier/repair effect and model‑call cost in an emulated multi‑vendor template setting.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 before any model calls. The primary estimand (confirmatory) is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the difference in probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable policy violations under guarded (GVR) minus baseline (single‑shot LLM). The preregistration, analysis plan, and planned exclusion/missingness rules are archived (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50). Task sampling and strata: the experiment used N = 200 unique operator intents sampled deterministically and stratified across 3 vendor‑template families and 4 topology patterns (12 strata) per the preregistered deterministic task_index_profile. Episodes per intent were paired: baseline and guarded. Shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics: the preregistration declared and the execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics—exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Because of this design, any paired difference for a given intent can only arise from deterministic validation outcomes and the permitted verifier‑triggered repair; baseline is the validator score on the shared initial candidate and guarded is the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. Model and sampling: the declared model identifier recorded in execution/model_configuration.json is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; explicitly, null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Budget and retry policy: preregistered limits were maximum_model_calls = 400, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Verification and repair: the deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 evaluated syntactic correctness, reachability/topology constraints, and encoded ACL/policy constraints derived from the task payloads; the guarded pipeline permitted up to one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent. Scoring and primary analysis: the binary per‑intent scoring rule declared in the preregistration labeled an episode as a 'success' when the final configuration passed the full intent constraint validation (no operationally detectable violations). The preregistered primary statistical test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired success indicators. Complementary exploratory analyses declared in the preregistration included a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra model calls per intent and per avoided violation). Missingness and exclusions: preregistered exclusion and missingness rules were applied (no pairs were excluded in the archived execution). Deterministic accounting and provider audit: the execution manifest records hosted_model_call_event_count = 204; decomposition and stage accounting (as audited) are 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls (repair stage_count = 4). The manifest records that cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 204; these audited counts are reported verbatim in Results for traceability.
sections.results: Execution and per‑intent outcomes: the run completed as preregistered (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200). The paired 2×2 contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02. Confirmatory test: the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary successes yields p = 0.125 (predeclared primary inference; do not reject at α = 0.05). Exploratory interval estimation: using the archived paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) we compute a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04] for the paired risk difference; per preregistration this bootstrap CI is exploratory and supplementary to the preregistered McNemar test. Repairs and cost accounting: four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the N = 200 intents (repair calls = 4). Total hosted model calls recorded = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repair calls). From these audited counts we compute mean hosted model calls per intent = 204/200 = 1.02; mean extra calls per intent due to guarded repairs = 0.02; mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0 (4 repair calls corresponding to 4 avoided baseline failures). Missingness and deviations: no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed; deterministic_reconciliation and episode accounting checks passed. Representative artifacts and validator traces: the archived execution/scoring and execution/responses entries show the same shared initial candidate used for both conditions for each pair (examples included in the evidence bundle substantiate the contingency counts). Statistical diagnostics and small‑discordance caution: the discordant count n10 + n01 = 4 is small; in such sparse‑discordance regimes exact conditional tests (McNemar) and resampling‑based intervals may give differing inference signals (as observed here). We therefore treat the McNemar test result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome and the bootstrap CI as an auxiliary descriptive estimator of effect magnitude.
sections.discussion: Confirmatory versus exploratory claims: by preregistration the exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired success indicators is the study's formal confirmatory inference; that test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). The paired bootstrap percentile CI is reported as exploratory and descriptive. The observed point estimate (paired risk difference = 0.02) and the exploratory bootstrap CI provide context on effect magnitude but do not change the preregistered confirmatory conclusion. Interpreting the shared_initial_candidate design: because exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was reused by baseline and guarded, baseline performance is the validator outcome on that shared draft and guarded performance is the final outcome after deterministic validation and allowed repair. Consequently, the observed paired improvements derive solely from deterministic verification and any permitted repair rather than from differences in first‑pass sampling or prompt engineering between arms; the design did not include an independent constrained‑prompt arm. Cost–benefit tradeoff: within this emulated, template‑driven setting a small repair budget (4 repairs over 200 intents) eliminated the mechanically detectable baseline violations in the archived workload, at a mean extra model‑call cost of 0.02 per intent. Operational implications are bounded: the result suggests that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides actionable localized feedback, modest repair budgets can eliminate mechanically checkable faults in similar template‑based emulated settings. Threats to validity and generalization: (1) Construct validity—our deterministic validator covers mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, encoded ACL/policy rules) but cannot guarantee detection of higher‑order semantic misinterpretations outside its encoded rule set. (2) External validity—the experiment used a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), Mininet‑style emulation, and synthetic vendor templates; findings do not directly imply equivalent performance on production hardware, other models, or in-the-field operator workflows. (3) Internal validity—the shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered and executed; this design prevents attributing improvements to prompt template modifications or constrained prompting that were not independently sampled. (4) Conclusion validity—the low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduces power to detect small absolute improvements; with sparse discordant pairs bootstrap intervals may exclude zero even when an exact conditional test does not reject, so effect interpretation must emphasize the preregistered confirmatory test. Recommendations for practice and follow‑up experiments: expand deterministic verifier coverage (semantic/policy ontologies), evaluate multiple hosted models and model versions to assess robustness to provider nondeterminism, and assess GVR pipelines against independent multi‑sample baselines to measure effects of prompting strategies; all follow‑ups should be preregistered and provenance‑traced.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) that measured whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact McNemar two‑sided) did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04]. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in this emulated template‑based setting. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator; further preregistered, multivendor/hardware evaluations with expanded verifier coverage are required.

disclosure_statement: Declared artifacts and autonomy: declared model gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5; deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; synthetic Mininet‑style harness. Preregistration: study preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) prior to any model calls. Initial master prompt: immutable initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Autonomy boundary and human role: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the lock the AI autonomously performed literature verification, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting. Generation semantics and temperature: execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by baseline and guarded; initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1); the archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial generation events + 4 repair calls (repair stage_count = 4). Reporting and provenance: reported counts and analysis artifacts are recorded in the archived execution and analysis bundles referenced above; no human manual editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
